topics.title: Who Is an Investment Adviser? Definitions & Exclusions
topics.reading:
The three-prong test

Both the Uniform Securities Act (USA) and the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 (IAA §202(a)(11)) define an investment adviser as any person who, for compensation, engages in the business of advising others, directly or through publications or writings, as to the value of securities or the advisability of investing in, purchasing, or selling securities, or who, for compensation and as part of a regular business, issues analyses or reports concerning securities. The SEC (Release IA-1092) boils this down to three prongs, and all three must be met:

  1. Advice about securities – advice limited to real estate, coins, fixed annuities, or commodities is not advice about securities. Advice on asset allocation among securities (stocks vs. bonds vs. mutual funds) is advice about securities.
  2. In the business – holding oneself out as an adviser, receiving separate compensation for advice, or giving specific advice other than on rare, isolated occasions.
  3. Compensation – any economic benefit, whether a separate fee, a wrap fee, or commissions on products sold as a result of the advice. It does not have to be called an "advisory fee."

"Person" includes individuals and entities (corporations, partnerships, LLCs, trusts). A financial planner, pension consultant, or sports/entertainment agent who advises clients on securities and is paid is generally an investment adviser.

Exclusions from the definition (USA)

A person who is excluded from the definition is simply not an investment adviser and never needs to register as one. Under the USA the term does not include:

  • Investment adviser representatives (they are covered by their own definition).
  • Banks, savings institutions, and trust companies (note: a bank holding company or a non-bank subsidiary is not automatically excluded).
  • LATE professionals – Lawyers, Accountants, Teachers, and Engineers whose advice is solely incidental to the practice of their profession. A CPA who opens a separate "investment advisory" service, advertises it, or charges separately for securities advice loses the exclusion.
  • Broker-dealers (and their agents) whose advice is solely incidental to their brokerage business and who receive no special compensation for it. A BD that charges a separate fee for a financial plan, or offers a wrap-fee program, is an adviser.
  • Publishers of any bona fide newspaper, news magazine, or business or financial publication of general, regular circulation that offers impersonal advice not tailored to any individual.
  • Federal covered advisers – advisers registered (or required to register) with the SEC are excluded from the USA's definition of investment adviser; the state's role is limited to notice filing.
  • Any other person the Administrator excludes by rule or order.

Exclusions under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940

The federal list is similar: banks and bank holding companies (with limits), LATE professionals, BDs with incidental advice and no special compensation, publishers of bona fide publications of general and regular circulation, persons whose advice relates only to U.S. government securities, family offices, and others designated by the SEC. The key difference to remember: the USA excludes federal covered advisers (because the state doesn't register them), while the IAA obviously does not.

PersonInvestment adviser?
Teacher who explains P/E ratios in a finance classNo – incidental to teaching
Teacher who sells a stock-picking newsletter to studentsYes – separate business for pay
Accountant who charges a fee for a retirement investment planYes – advice is not solely incidental
BD that charges a separate fee for financial plansYes – special compensation
Weekly financial newspaper of general circulationNo – bona fide publisher
Newsletter whose content is timed to market events and sent to a select listYes – not bona fide/general and regular
Bank trust departmentNo – bank exclusion
Exam tip: For "who is an investment adviser" questions, first ask whether the person is excluded. If the person is a lawyer, accountant, teacher, or engineer, look for the words "solely incidental." If the stem mentions a separate fee, advertising investment advice, or holding out as a financial planner, the exclusion is lost.
Trap: "Excluded" and "exempt" are different. An excluded person is not an investment adviser at all. An exempt adviser (e.g., the de minimis rule) is an investment adviser but need not register in a particular state — and remains subject to the antifraud provisions.
keyPoints: IA definition requires all three prongs: advice about securities, in the business, for compensation.
Compensation includes any economic benefit, including commissions — not only a separate advisory fee.
USA exclusions: IARs, banks/savings institutions/trust companies, LATE (solely incidental), BDs (incidental + no special compensation), bona fide publishers, federal covered advisers.
A BD loses its exclusion if it receives special compensation, e.g., a separate fee for a financial plan or a wrap fee.
Publishers must offer impersonal advice in a publication of general and regular circulation; a timed or select-audience newsletter doesn't qualify.
Excluded persons are not advisers at all; exempt advisers are advisers who are relieved from registration in a state but remain subject to antifraud rules.

topics.title: State vs. SEC Registration, Notice Filing & Exemptions
topics.reading:
Who registers where?

Since the National Securities Markets Improvement Act of 1996 (NSMIA) and the Dodd-Frank Act (2010), regulation of advisers is split between the SEC and the states, mainly by regulatory assets under management (AUM):

AdviserWhere it registers
Small adviser, under $25 million AUMState (generally prohibited from SEC registration)
Mid-sized adviser, $25 million to $100 millionState, if required to register with and subject to examination by its home state
$100 million to $110 million (buffer)May choose SEC registration (optional)
$110 million or moreMust register with the SEC
Adviser to a registered investment company (mutual fund) or business development companySEC, regardless of AUM

Once registered with the SEC, an adviser need not switch back to state registration unless its AUM falls below $90 million (reported on the annual updating amendment). Other advisers that may or must register with the SEC despite low AUM include advisers that would otherwise have to register in 15 or more states, certain pension consultants, internet advisers, and advisers affiliated with an SEC-registered adviser.

Federal covered advisers and notice filing

An SEC-registered adviser is a federal covered adviser. States cannot require it to register, but a state may require a notice filing: copies of documents filed with the SEC (Form ADV), a filing fee, and a consent to service of process. Notice filings are made electronically through the Investment Adviser Registration Depository (IARD). States retain full antifraud authority over federal covered advisers — a state can investigate and bring an enforcement action for fraud or deceit, but cannot impose its own net worth, books-and-records, or registration requirements on them.

Exemptions from state registration (de minimis)

An investment adviser that is not SEC-registered must register in a state unless an exemption applies. Under the USA, an adviser is exempt from registration in a state if it has no place of business in the state and either:

  • its only clients in the state are institutional — other investment advisers, federal covered advisers, broker-dealers, banks, savings institutions, trust companies, insurance companies, investment companies, employee benefit plans meeting asset thresholds, and similar institutions; or
  • during the preceding 12 months it has had no more than 5 clients who are residents of the state, other than the institutional clients above.

Under NSMIA the de minimis rule is a national standard: a state may not require registration of an adviser with no place of business in the state and fewer than 6 resident clients in the preceding 12 months. "No more than 5" and "fewer than 6" mean the same thing. The moment the adviser establishes a place of business (an office, or any location it holds out as a place where advisory services are provided — including a home office) in the state, the exemption is lost regardless of client count.

Federal exemptions for private fund advisers

Some advisers are exempt from SEC registration but still file abbreviated reports on Form ADV as exempt reporting advisers (ERAs):

  • Private fund adviser exemption – advises solely private funds (e.g., hedge funds) and has less than $150 million in regulatory AUM in the United States.
  • Venture capital fund adviser exemption – advises solely venture capital funds, with no AUM limit.

Other federal exemptions include foreign private advisers and intrastate advisers (all clients in the home state, and no advice on listed securities). Family offices are excluded from the definition entirely. An ERA may still have to register with a state unless the state provides an exemption.

Exam tip: Work in order: (1) Is the person an adviser at all (exclusions)? (2) Is it federal covered? If so, the state only gets a notice filing. (3) If state-regulated, does it have a place of business in this state? If yes, register. If no, count non-institutional resident clients over the past 12 months — 5 or fewer means no registration needed in that state.
Trap: Advisers to registered investment companies register with the SEC even if they manage only $5 million. Also, "institutional" clients do not count toward the 5-client limit — an out-of-state adviser with 3 individuals and 40 pension plans as clients is still exempt.
keyPoints: Generally: under $100M AUM → state; $100M–$110M → may choose SEC; $110M or more → must register with SEC.
SEC-registered advisers may stay with SEC until AUM falls below $90M.
Advisers to registered investment companies register with the SEC regardless of AUM.
States may require federal covered advisers to notice file: copies of SEC filings, a fee, and consent to service of process.
De minimis: no place of business in the state AND no more than 5 non-institutional resident clients in 12 months → no state registration.
An adviser whose only clients in the state are institutions (and no place of business there) need not register.
Private fund advisers with less than $150M and venture capital fund advisers are exempt reporting advisers, not SEC-registered.
States keep antifraud authority over all advisers, including federal covered and exempt advisers.

topics.title: IA Registration Process, Form ADV, Net Worth & Records
topics.reading:
Applying for registration

A state-registered investment adviser applies on Form ADV, filed electronically through IARD, along with a filing fee and a consent to service of process. Form ADV has two parts:

  • Part 1 – regulatory information: ownership, AUM, business activities, disciplinary history. Filed with regulators and publicly available.
  • Part 2A (the firm brochure) – a plain-English narrative of services, fees, conflicts of interest, methods of analysis, disciplinary information, and more.
  • Part 2B (brochure supplement) – information about the specific individuals (IARs) who provide advice to the client: education, business experience, disciplinary history, other business activities, and supervision.

Under the USA, if no denial or other proceeding is pending, registration becomes effective at noon on the 30th day after a complete application is filed (the Administrator may make it effective sooner). Registrations expire December 31 each year unless renewed. The Administrator may require that an applicant (or its IARs) pass a qualifying exam such as the Series 65.

Keeping Form ADV current

  • Annual updating amendment – within 90 days after the end of the adviser's fiscal year.
  • Other-than-annual amendments – promptly when certain information becomes inaccurate (e.g., change of address, disciplinary events, material changes to the brochure).
  • Form ADV-W – used to withdraw registration. Under the USA a withdrawal becomes effective 30 days after filing unless a revocation or suspension proceeding is pending; the Administrator may still start a revocation proceeding within one year after the withdrawal became effective.

Delivering the brochure

Under NASAA's model rule (the "brochure rule"), a state-registered adviser must deliver Part 2A and the relevant 2B supplements to a new client either:

  • at least 48 hours before entering into the advisory contract, or
  • at the time of entering into the contract, if the client has the right to terminate the contract without penalty within 5 business days.

Each year, within 120 days after fiscal year-end, the adviser must deliver, free of charge, either an updated brochure that includes or comes with a summary of material changes, or the summary with an offer to provide the updated brochure (NASAA's model rule mirrors the SEC rule for federal covered advisers). Brochure delivery is not required for clients who receive only impersonal advice and pay less than $500 a year.

Net worth and bonding (NASAA model rule)

State-registered adviser that…Minimum net worth
Has custody of client funds or securities$35,000
Has discretionary authority but not custody$10,000
Accepts prepayment of more than $500 per client, 6 or more months in advancePositive net worth at all times

An adviser that does not meet its net worth requirement may instead post a surety bond covering the deficiency (rounded up to the nearest $5,000). An adviser whose principal office is in another state need only satisfy its home state's net worth requirement. If net worth drops below the minimum, the adviser must notify the Administrator by the close of the next business day and file a financial report. Federal covered advisers are not subject to state net worth or bonding requirements — NSMIA preempts them.

Books and records

State-registered advisers must keep books and records (client agreements, trade records, written communications about recommendations, advertisements, financial statements, etc.) for 5 years from the end of the fiscal year of the last entry, the first 2 years in an easily accessible place (the adviser's principal office). Records may be kept electronically. The Administrator may inspect records at any time, without prior notice. A state may not require a federal covered adviser to keep records beyond what the SEC requires.

Supervision

An adviser must establish, maintain, and enforce written supervisory procedures reasonably designed to prevent violations by its IARs and employees. Failure to reasonably supervise an IAR is a ground for denying, suspending, or revoking the adviser's registration.

Exam tip: Memorize the number set: 30 days (effectiveness), 90 days (annual ADV update), 48 hours / 5 business days (brochure), $35,000 custody / $10,000 discretion / $500 and 6 months prepayment, 5 years / 2 easily accessible (records), December 31 (renewal).
Trap: Discretion requires $10,000; custody requires $35,000. An adviser with both custody and discretion needs $35,000, not $45,000. And the prepayment test needs both conditions: more than $500 and 6 or more months in advance.
keyPoints: Form ADV Part 1 = regulatory info; Part 2A = brochure; Part 2B = supplement about the individuals giving advice.
State registration effective at noon on the 30th day after filing if no proceeding is pending; registrations expire December 31.
Annual updating amendment is due within 90 days of fiscal year-end; material changes are amended promptly; Form ADV-W withdraws.

Brochure: deliver 48 hours before the contract, or at signing with a 5-business-day penalty-free cancellation right; annually (within 120 days of fiscal year-end) deliver an updated brochure or a summary of material changes with an offer.
Net worth: custody $35,000; discretion only $10,000; prepayment over $500 and 6+ months ahead → positive net worth; a bond may cover a deficiency.
Federal covered advisers are not subject to state net worth, bonding, or extra books-and-records requirements.
IA records: 5 years, first 2 in an easily accessible place; Administrator may inspect without notice.

topics.title: Investment Adviser Representatives (IARs)
topics.reading:
Definition

Under the USA, an investment adviser representative is any partner, officer, director, or other individual employed by or associated with an investment adviser (state-registered or federal covered) who does any of the following:

  • makes any recommendations or otherwise renders advice regarding securities;
  • manages accounts or portfolios of clients;
  • determines which recommendation or advice should be given;
  • solicits, offers, or negotiates for the sale of, or sells, investment advisory services (including solicitors paid to bring in clients); or
  • supervises employees who do any of the above.

Individuals who perform only clerical or ministerial functions — a receptionist, a secretary who types reports, a back-office employee who processes paperwork — are not IARs. Only individuals can be IARs; a firm is never an IAR.

Registration

IARs register with the state by filing Form U4 through the Central Registration Depository (CRD). Registration generally requires passing the Series 65 (or Series 7 + Series 66). Like other registrations, it becomes effective at noon on the 30th day if nothing is pending and expires December 31 unless renewed.

IARs of state-registered advisers must be registered in the states where they conduct advisory business. If the adviser itself is exempt from registration in a state under the de minimis rule (no place of business, 5 or fewer non-institutional clients), its IARs need not register there either.

IARs of federal covered advisers: under NSMIA, a state may require an IAR of an SEC-registered adviser to register only if the IAR has a place of business in that state. An IAR of a federal covered adviser who lives and works in State A and has clients in States B and C registers only in State A.

Unlawful to employ unregistered IARs

It is unlawful for a state-registered investment adviser to employ an IAR who is not registered (or exempt), and unlawful for a federal covered adviser to employ, supervise, or associate with an individual who is required to be registered as an IAR in a state but isn't.

Termination and transfer

  • When an IAR of a state-registered adviser begins or terminates association, the investment adviser must promptly notify the Administrator.
  • For an IAR of a federal covered adviser, the change is reported through the CRD system (Form U5 on termination), since the state does not register the firm itself.
  • An IAR's registration is not effective while the individual is not associated with an adviser.

Dual roles

Many individuals are both agents of a broker-dealer and IARs of an affiliated adviser. Each role requires its own registration. An agent who begins charging a separate fee for advice, or who works for a dually registered firm's advisory business, must also be registered as an IAR. Supervisors of IARs are themselves IARs and must register.

IndividualIAR?
Employee who decides which securities go on the firm's recommended listYes – determines advice
Salesperson who markets the firm's advisory services for a commissionYes – solicits advisory services
Office manager who supervises portfolio managersYes – supervises
Receptionist who schedules client meetingsNo – clerical
Employee who mails out the firm's printed newsletterNo – ministerial
Exam tip: Place of business is the trigger for IARs of federal covered advisers. For IARs of state advisers, think "wherever the firm must register, the IARs doing business there must register too."
Trap: The firm may be a federal covered adviser that the state cannot register, while its IAR must still register with the state where the IAR has a place of business. Don't assume SEC registration of the firm covers the individual.
keyPoints: IAR = individual who gives advice, manages accounts, determines advice, solicits advisory services, or supervises those who do.
Clerical and ministerial personnel are not IARs; only individuals can be IARs.
IARs register on Form U4 through CRD; Series 65 (or 7 + 66) generally required.
States may require IARs of federal covered advisers to register only where they have a place of business.
For IARs of state-registered advisers, the adviser must promptly notify the Administrator when the IAR begins or ends association.
It is unlawful for an adviser to employ an IAR who is required to be registered and is not.

topics.title: Broker-Dealers: Definition, Exclusions & Registration
topics.reading:
Definition

Under the USA, a broker-dealer is any person engaged in the business of effecting transactions in securities for the account of others (acting as a broker/agent for customers) or for its own account (acting as a dealer/principal). Only firms matter here in practice; the individuals who work for them are agents.

Exclusions (not a broker-dealer)

  • Agents – individuals who represent a BD or issuer.
  • Issuers – a company selling its own securities is an issuer, not a BD.
  • Banks, savings institutions, and trust companies.
  • A person with no place of business in the state whose only transactions in the state are with issuers of the securities involved, other broker-dealers, or institutional investors (banks, insurance companies, investment companies, pension or profit-sharing trusts, and similar financial institutions).
  • A BD with no place of business in the state that deals with an existing customer who is only temporarily present in the state (for example, a client on vacation), provided the BD is registered in the customer's home state. The 2002 Act's version of this "snowbird" provision limits the visit to a short period (commonly taught as 30 days).

Note that a BD with no place of business in the state that solicits even one individual (non-institutional) resident who is not covered by the existing-customer rule must register. There is no "5-client" de minimis rule for broker-dealers.

Related terms

  • Underwriter – a BD that purchases securities from an issuer with a view to distribution, or offers/sells for an issuer in connection with a distribution. Transactions between an issuer and an underwriter are exempt transactions.
  • Market maker – a dealer that stands ready to buy and sell a particular security for its own account, continuously quoting bid and ask prices.
  • Associated person – any partner, officer, director, branch manager, employee, or person controlling or controlled by the BD. Associated persons who sell securities are agents.
  • Principal – on registration forms, officers, directors, and supervisors of the firm; in trading, a BD acting as dealer from its own inventory.

Registration

A BD registers with the state by filing Form BD through CRD, with a filing fee and a consent to service of process. When a BD registers, its partners, officers, and directors who act as agents are automatically registered as agents (under the 1956 Act). Registration is effective at noon on the 30th day if no proceeding is pending and expires December 31.

Financial and record requirements

  • Net capital – set by SEC Rule 15c3-1. Under NSMIA, a state may not impose net capital, custody, margin, financial responsibility, books-and-records, or reporting requirements on BDs that differ from or exceed the SEC's.
  • Surety bonds – the Administrator may require a bond, but a BD that meets SEC net capital rules cannot be required to exceed federal standards.
  • Records – under SEC rules most BD records (blotters, customer account records, order tickets, communications) must be kept at least 3 years, the first 2 in an easily accessible place; some records (e.g., ledgers, partnership articles) must be kept 6 years or for the life of the firm.
  • Financial reports – BDs file periodic financial reports (e.g., FOCUS reports) and an annual audited financial statement, and must send customers a balance sheet.
Exam tip: For BD questions, look for a place of business. With no place of business, the BD may deal in the state only with issuers, other BDs, institutions, and certain existing customers temporarily present. Any other retail customer requires registration.
Trap: Don't carry over the IA de minimis rule. An investment adviser can have up to 5 non-institutional clients without registering in a state; a broker-dealer cannot sell to a single new retail resident without registering.
keyPoints: A broker-dealer effects securities transactions for others (broker) or for its own account (dealer).
Excluded: agents, issuers, banks/savings institutions/trust companies, and firms with no place of business dealing only with issuers, other BDs, or institutions.
An existing customer temporarily present in the state (vacationing) may be served without registering in that state if the BD is registered in the customer's home state.
There is no 5-client de minimis exemption for broker-dealers.
Underwriter = distributes for an issuer; market maker = continuously quotes bid/ask for its own account.
States may not impose net capital, books-and-records, or financial reporting requirements on BDs beyond SEC rules.
Most BD records are kept 3 years, first 2 easily accessible.

topics.title: Agents: Definition, Exclusions & Registration
topics.reading:
Definition

An agent is any individual (never a firm) other than a broker-dealer who represents a broker-dealer or an issuer in effecting or attempting to effect purchases or sales of securities. Partners, officers, and directors of a BD or issuer are agents only if they perform similar functions.

Individuals who are NOT agents

An individual representing an issuer is not an agent when effecting transactions:

  • in certain exempt securities – e.g., U.S. and foreign government securities, municipal securities, bank and savings institution securities, and qualifying commercial paper;
  • in exempt transactions (for example, a private placement or a sale to institutional investors);
  • with existing employees, partners, or directors of the issuer under an employee benefit plan, if no commission or other remuneration is paid for soliciting them.

Also not agents: clerical and ministerial personnel of a BD, such as receptionists and back-office staff. On the exam, anyone who solicits or accepts orders for a BD is an agent; anyone who performs only clerical work is not.

Crucially, an individual representing a broker-dealer in securities transactions is always an agent, even when selling exempt securities (e.g., municipal bonds) or effecting exempt transactions. The exclusion for exempt securities/transactions applies only to individuals representing issuers.

Registration

  • Agents register via Form U4 through CRD, filed by the sponsoring BD or issuer, and typically must pass the Series 63 or 66 (plus FINRA exams where required).
  • An agent may represent only one BD or one issuer at a time, unless the BDs or issuers are affiliated by direct or indirect common control.
  • An agent's registration is not effective during any period when the agent is not associated with a registered BD or issuer.
  • Registration is effective at noon on the 30th day if no proceeding is pending, and expires December 31.

Termination and transfer

When an agent begins or terminates a connection with a BD or issuer, both the agent and the BD (or issuer) must promptly notify the Administrator. When an agent moves from BD A to BD B, three parties notify: BD A, BD B, and the agent. The termination is reported to CRD on Form U5, and the new firm files a new U4.

Where must an agent register?

An agent must be registered in each state in which he or she transacts business with persons who are not excluded (e.g., institutions). If the BD is not required to register in a state (e.g., it deals only with institutions there), its agents need not register there either. An agent who calls a new individual customer in another state must be registered in that state — along with the BD.

IndividualAgent?
Employee of a BD selling Treasury bonds to retail customersYes – always an agent when representing a BD
Issuer's officer selling its commercial paper to the public, no commissionNo – issuer + exempt security
Issuer's employee selling its stock in a registered public offering for a commissionYes – non-exempt issuer transaction
Issuer's HR staff offering stock to employees in a benefit plan, no commissionNo
BD's receptionist who only answers phonesNo – clerical
Exam tip: Ask "whom does the individual represent?" BD → agent (unless purely clerical). Issuer → agent only when the security and the transaction are both non-exempt (and not the no-commission employee plan).
Trap: Nonprofit (e.g., church) bonds are exempt securities, but an individual representing the issuer in selling them is not automatically excluded from the agent definition — the issuer-agent exclusion covers only certain exempt securities (government, municipal, foreign government, bank, and commercial paper). Don't assume "exempt security" always means "not an agent."
keyPoints: An agent is an individual (never a firm) who represents a BD or issuer in effecting securities transactions.
An individual representing a broker-dealer is always an agent, even for exempt securities or transactions (clerical staff excepted).
An issuer's representative is not an agent when selling certain exempt securities, in exempt transactions, or to employees under a benefit plan with no commission.
Agents register on Form U4; an agent may represent only one BD or issuer at a time unless they are under common control.
Agent registration is not effective while the agent is unaffiliated with a BD or issuer.
On termination, both the agent and the BD/issuer must promptly notify the Administrator; on transfer, the old firm, new firm, and agent notify.

topics.title: Securities, Issuers & Registration Methods
topics.reading:
What is a security?

The USA defines "security" broadly: stocks, bonds, notes, debentures, evidences of indebtedness, certificates of interest in profit-sharing agreements, preorganization certificates or subscriptions, transferable shares, investment contracts, voting-trust certificates, certificates of deposit for a security, fractional interests in oil, gas, or mineral rights, puts, calls, straddles, options, warrants, and variable annuities. The catch-all is the investment contract, defined by the Supreme Court's Howey test:

  1. an investment of money
  2. in a common enterprise
  3. with an expectation of profits
  4. derived primarily from the efforts of others.

Under this test, interests in limited partnerships, many cryptocurrency offerings, whiskey-warehouse receipts, and pay-telephone or viatical programs have been held to be securities.

What is NOT a security

  • Fixed annuities and other insurance or endowment policies that promise a fixed sum (variable annuities are securities)
  • Commodities and commodity futures contracts
  • Collectibles – art, coins, precious metals held directly, rare stamps
  • Interests in a retirement plan (e.g., a participant's interest in a 401(k) or pension plan) – the plan's underlying investments may be securities, but the participant's interest itself is not
  • Real estate held directly (such as a home), and bank checking or savings accounts

Issuers and issuer vs. nonissuer transactions

An issuer is any person who issues or proposes to issue a security. For certificates of deposit, voting-trust certificates, or collateral-trust certificates, the issuer is the person performing the acts and assuming the duties of the depositor or manager. An issuer transaction is one in which the proceeds benefit the issuer (primary offerings). A nonissuer transaction is not for the direct or indirect benefit of the issuer — essentially secondary market trading.

Why registration matters

Under the USA it is unlawful to offer or sell any security in a state unless it is (1) registered, (2) a federal covered security, or (3) exempt (or sold in an exempt transaction).

The three state registration methods

MethodWho uses itEffective
Notification (filing)Established issuers with a history of operations and earnings (under the 1956 Act; the 2002 Act largely replaced it with notice filing for federal covered securities)Automatically after a short waiting period (3:00 p.m. on the second full business day under the 1956 Act) unless the Administrator acts
CoordinationIssuers simultaneously registering with the SEC under the Securities Act of 1933At the same moment the federal registration becomes effective, if conditions are met
QualificationAny security; used for offerings not registered with the SEC, such as intrastate offeringsWhen the Administrator so orders

A registration statement may be filed by the issuer, any other person on whose behalf the offering is made, or a registered BD. The Administrator may require that proceeds be escrowed or impounded, that securities issued to promoters be escrowed, and that a prospectus be delivered; qualification is the most demanding method. Registrations under the USA generally remain effective for one year from the effective date.

Federal covered securities

NSMIA created federal covered securities, which states may not require to be registered:

  • Securities listed (or authorized for listing) on the NYSE, Nasdaq, and other national exchanges, plus securities of the same issuer equal or senior to them (e.g., its bonds and preferred)
  • Securities of investment companies registered under the Investment Company Act of 1940 (mutual funds, UITs, closed-end funds)
  • Securities sold in Rule 506 of Regulation D private placements
  • Securities sold to qualified purchasers, most securities exempt from registration under Section 3(a) of the 1933 Act (other than municipal securities of in-state issuers), and Regulation A Tier 2 offerings

States may still require notice filings and fees (for example, a notice filing and fee for investment company shares, or a Form D for a Rule 506 offering), and keep full antifraud authority.

Exam tip: Coordination = "coordinated with the SEC." Qualification = "the only method available for an intrastate offering that won't be registered with the SEC." Notification = "seasoned issuer with an earnings history."
Trap: A variable annuity is a security (and an investment company product); a fixed annuity is not. A 401(k) plan interest is not a security, even though the mutual funds inside the plan are.
keyPoints: Howey test: investment of money, common enterprise, expectation of profits, primarily from the efforts of others.
Not securities: fixed annuities and insurance, commodities/futures, collectibles, retirement plan interests, directly owned real estate.
Variable annuities, options, warrants, and fractional oil and gas interests are securities.
It is unlawful to sell a security in a state unless it is registered, federal covered, or exempt (or sold in an exempt transaction).
Registration methods: notification (seasoned issuers), coordination (concurrent SEC registration), qualification (all others, e.g., intrastate; effective when the Administrator orders).
Federal covered: exchange-listed securities, registered investment company shares, Rule 506 private placements; states may require notice filings and fees only.
Issuer transaction benefits the issuer (primary); nonissuer transaction does not (secondary).

topics.title: Exempt Securities vs. Exempt Transactions
topics.reading:
Two different kinds of exemption

An exempt security is exempt because of the nature of its issuer — it can be sold without state registration no matter who buys it or how often it trades. An exempt transaction is exempt because of the manner of the sale or the type of buyer — the security itself is not exempt, only that particular transaction is. The same share of stock can be sold in an exempt transaction today and require registration tomorrow.

Neither type of exemption relieves anyone from the antifraud provisions. The Administrator has antifraud jurisdiction over all securities and transactions, including federal covered and exempt ones. And an exemption from securities registration does not exempt the person selling from agent or BD registration.

Exempt securities (USA §402(a) / §201)

  • U.S. government and agency securities (Treasuries, GNMAs)
  • Municipal securities – any state, political subdivision, or public authority
  • Securities of foreign governments with which the U.S. maintains diplomatic relations, and Canadian government and provincial securities
  • Securities issued or guaranteed by banks, savings institutions, and trust companies (and credit unions/building and loan associations) supervised by a state or federal authority
  • Securities of insurance companies authorized to do business in the state (not variable annuities)
  • Securities of federally regulated public utilities and common carriers
  • Federal covered securities, including exchange-listed securities
  • Securities of nonprofit religious, educational, charitable, fraternal, or benevolent organizations
  • Commercial paper rated in one of the three highest rating categories (prime quality), with a maturity of not more than 9 months (270 days), in denominations of at least $50,000
  • Investment contracts in connection with qualified employee pension, profit-sharing, or stock bonus plans

Exempt transactions (USA §402(b) / §202)

  • Isolated nonissuer transactions – occasional private resales, whether or not through a BD
  • Unsolicited nonissuer transactions effected through a registered BD (the Administrator may require the customer to acknowledge in writing that the order was unsolicited)
  • Transactions between an issuer and an underwriter, or among underwriters
  • Offers or sales to institutional investors – banks, savings institutions, trust companies, insurance companies, investment companies, pension or profit-sharing trusts, and BDs
  • Private placements – offers directed to no more than 10 persons in the state (not counting institutional buyers) during any 12 consecutive months, the seller reasonably believes buyers are purchasing for investment, and no commission is paid for soliciting non-institutional buyers
  • Transactions by fiduciaries – executors, administrators, sheriffs, marshals, receivers, trustees in bankruptcy, guardians, or conservators
  • Pledges – a bona fide pledgee (lender) selling collateral to satisfy a debt
  • Preorganization subscriptions – no more than 10 subscribers, no commission, and no payment by subscribers
  • Rights offerings to existing security holders, if no commission is paid for soliciting (other than a standby commission)
  • Nonissuer transactions in securities listed in a recognized securities manual (the "manual exemption"), under stated conditions

Investment companies (Investment Company Act of 1940)

Investment company securities registered under the 1940 Act are federal covered. The 1940 Act classifies investment companies as:

  • Face-amount certificate companies – issue debt certificates that pay a stated face amount at maturity in exchange for periodic or lump-sum payments.
  • Unit investment trusts (UITs) – organized under a trust indenture, have no board of directors, issue redeemable units in a fixed, largely unmanaged portfolio.
  • Management companies – actively managed; open-end (mutual funds, continuously offering redeemable shares) or closed-end (fixed number of shares trading in the secondary market).
Exam tip: If the answer depends on who issued it (government, municipality, bank, insurer, nonprofit), it's an exempt security. If it depends on who is buying, who is selling, or how (institution, fiduciary, pledgee, unsolicited, isolated, 10 offerees), it's an exempt transaction.
Trap: Commercial paper must satisfy all conditions — prime rating, 9 months or less, and $50,000 minimum denomination. A 12-month note from a top-rated company is not exempt commercial paper. And private placement counts offerees, not buyers: offering to 15 individuals violates the exemption even if only 3 buy.
keyPoints: Exempt securities are exempt because of the issuer; exempt transactions are exempt because of the buyer or manner of sale.
Exempt securities: U.S. government, municipal, foreign governments with diplomatic relations, banks, insurance companies, utilities, nonprofits, qualifying commercial paper, federal covered.
Commercial paper: prime rating (top 3), maturity 9 months or less, denominations of $50,000 or more.
Exempt transactions: isolated nonissuer, unsolicited nonissuer, issuer-underwriter, institutional, private placement, fiduciary, pledgee, preorganization, rights offerings.
Private placement: offers to no more than 10 non-institutional persons in the state in 12 months, investment intent, no commission to solicit non-institutional buyers.
Antifraud provisions apply to all securities and transactions, including exempt and federal covered.
Investment company types: face-amount certificate companies, UITs, management companies (open-end and closed-end).

topics.title: Administrator Powers, Jurisdiction & Penalties
topics.reading:
Powers of the Administrator

The Administrator is the state official or agency that administers the state securities act. The Administrator may:

  • Investigate, publicly or privately, inside or outside the state, and publish information about violations.
  • Issue subpoenas, administer oaths, take testimony, and require production of books and records. If a person refuses a subpoena, the Administrator must ask a court to compel compliance (contempt).
  • Make, amend, and rescind rules, forms, and orders; define terms; and issue interpretive opinions (for a fee).
  • Deny, suspend, or revoke registrations of BDs, agents, IAs, IARs, and securities.
  • Issue cease and desist orders, including summary orders issued without a prior hearing, followed by an opportunity for a hearing. The Administrator cannot issue injunctions or impose prison sentences — those require a court.
  • Censure registrants, impose bars, and (under the 2002 Act) impose civil penalties.

Before a final order to deny, suspend, or revoke, the Administrator must give appropriate prior notice, an opportunity for a hearing, and written findings of fact and conclusions of law. A summary suspension or postponement may be entered pending that final determination.

Grounds for denial, suspension, or revocation

An order must be in the public interest AND the registrant must have done something that is a ground, such as:

  • filing an application that is incomplete or false/misleading in a material respect
  • willfully violating or willfully failing to comply with the Act
  • being convicted within the past 10 years of any securities-related misdemeanor or any felony
  • being permanently or temporarily enjoined by a court from securities activity
  • being subject to an order of another state's Administrator, the SEC, or an SRO denying or revoking registration
  • engaging in dishonest or unethical practices; being insolvent
  • not being qualified on the basis of training, experience, and knowledge
  • failing to reasonably supervise agents or IARs; failing to pay a filing fee (denial only, lifted when paid)

Lack of experience alone is not a ground if the person is qualified by training or knowledge. A nonpunitive cancellation is used when a registrant no longer exists, has ceased doing business, cannot be located, or has been adjudicated mentally incompetent.

Jurisdiction: when is an offer "in this state"?

  • An offer is made in the state when it originates from the state, or is directed to the state and received there.
  • An offer is accepted in the state when acceptance is communicated to the offeror in the state.
  • An offer is not made in a state merely because it appears in a bona fide newspaper published outside the state, or one published inside the state that had more than 2/3 of its circulation outside the state during the past 12 months, or is broadcast on radio/TV originating outside the state.

Criminal penalties

Under the 1956 USA, a person who willfully violates the Act may be fined up to $5,000, imprisoned up to 3 years, or both, per violation. No one may be imprisoned for violating a rule or order if the person proves no knowledge of it. Only the courts impose criminal penalties; the Administrator refers cases to the attorney general or prosecutor.

Civil liabilities

A buyer may sue a seller who (a) sold a security in violation of the Act (e.g., unregistered security or unregistered agent) or (b) sold by means of a material misrepresentation or omission. If the buyer still owns the security, the remedy is rescission:

Recovery = purchase price + interest at the legal rate + court costs + reasonable attorney's fees − any income received (dividends/interest).

If the buyer no longer owns the security, the buyer may recover damages. Advisory clients harmed by violations may similarly recover the advisory fees paid plus interest, costs, and attorney's fees, less income. Partners, officers, directors, and employees who materially aid the violation are jointly and severally liable unless they did not know and could not reasonably have known. A cause of action survives the death of either party.

Statute of limitations (as tested): the earlier of 2 years after discovery of the violation or 3 years after the sale. A buyer who receives a written rescission offer and fails to accept it within 30 days loses the right to sue.

Other key provisions

  • Any condition or stipulation requiring a buyer to waive compliance with the Act is void.
  • Registration does not mean the Administrator has approved the security or passed on the merits or the registrant's qualifications. It is unlawful to represent that it has.
Exam tip: Administrator = administrative actions (orders, subpoenas, denials). Courts = injunctions, compelling subpoenas, fines/jail, civil awards. "Willful" is the trigger for criminal liability.
Trap: The rescission formula subtracts income received and adds interest and attorney's fees. And a rescission offer only cuts off the lawsuit if the buyer fails to accept within 30 days.
keyPoints: Administrator may investigate in or outside the state, subpoena, deny/suspend/revoke, issue cease and desist and summary orders — but courts issue injunctions and criminal penalties.
A deny/suspend/revoke order requires both public interest and a statutory ground; final orders need notice, opportunity for hearing, and written findings.
Nonpunitive cancellation: registrant no longer exists, ceased business, cannot be located, or adjudicated mentally incompetent.
Offer made in the state when it originates there or is directed to and received there; accepted when acceptance is communicated to the offeror in the state.
Criminal (1956 Act): willful violations only — up to $5,000 fine and/or 3 years in prison.
Rescission: purchase price + interest + costs + attorney's fees − income received.
Civil suits: earlier of 2 years from discovery or 3 years from sale; rejecting a rescission offer for 30 days ends the right to sue.
Waivers of compliance are void; representing that the Administrator approved a registration is unlawful.

topics.title: Client Communications, Disclosures & Advisory Contracts
topics.reading:
The standard: no misleading statements

The antifraud provisions of the Uniform Securities Act (USA) and Section 206 of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 make it unlawful, in connection with investment advice or the offer or sale of a security, to make an untrue statement of a material fact or to leave out a material fact needed to keep a statement from being misleading. It covers everything a firm or its representatives say or write to clients. The antifraud rules apply even when the person or the security is exempt from registration.

Required disclosures

  • Form ADV Part 2A (the brochure) describes the firm's services, fees, conflicts of interest, disciplinary history and business practices in plain English. Part 2B (the brochure supplement) covers each IAR who gives the client advice.
  • Delivery under the NASAA model rule (state-registered advisers): deliver the brochure at least 48 hours before the client signs the advisory contract, or at signing if the client can cancel without penalty within 5 business days.
  • SEC-registered advisers deliver the brochure before or at the time the contract is signed. Each year, within 120 days after fiscal year-end, they deliver either an updated brochure or a summary of material changes with an offer to provide the brochure.
  • Conflicts, such as commissions on recommended products, soft-dollar benefits and affiliated firms, must be disclosed. So must material disciplinary events.

Unlawful representations

  • Registration is not approval. It is unlawful to say or imply that the Administrator or the SEC has passed on the merits of, recommended or approved any person, security or transaction. "We are registered with the State Securities Division" is a factual statement. "Our strategy is approved by the State" is a violation. Putting "RIA" after a name as if it were a professional degree is also misleading.
  • Titles and designations. Misrepresenting your qualifications, experience or credentials is unethical. NASAA's model rule on senior-specific certifications makes it misleading to use a title such as "certified senior adviser" when it implies special training the person does not have, or when it comes from an organization that is not properly accredited. Under Advisers Act Section 208(c), an adviser may call itself "investment counsel" only if advising is its principal business and a substantial part of that business is providing investment supervisory services.
  • Guarantees. Promising a client a specific result, or guaranteeing a client against loss, is prohibited. You may call a security "guaranteed" only when a third party, such as the U.S. government, a parent company or an insurer, actually guarantees payment of principal and/or interest.

Advisory contracts

Under the NASAA statement of policy on unethical practices, it is unethical to enter into, extend or renew an advisory contract that is not in writing. The written contract must disclose:

  • the services to be provided
  • the term of the contract
  • the advisory fee and the formula for computing it
  • how much of any prepaid fee is refunded if the contract ends early
  • whether the contract grants discretionary power
  • that the contract cannot be assigned without the client's consent

The USA also requires every advisory contract to provide that:

  1. the adviser will not be paid on the basis of capital gains or appreciation (a performance fee), except as permitted by rule, which means only for qualified clients;
  2. the adviser will not assign the contract without the client's consent;
  3. if the adviser is a partnership, it will notify the client of any change in the partnership's membership within a reasonable time.

Assignment includes any direct or indirect transfer of the contract, including the transfer of a controlling block of the adviser's voting stock. When a minority of a partnership's partners changes (for example, a junior partner retires or a new one is admitted), there is no assignment, so client consent is not needed, but clients must be notified. A change of control (a majority) is an assignment and needs client consent.

Trap: Federal law (the Advisers Act) does not technically require a written advisory contract, but NASAA does. On the Series 65, the answer is that the contract must be in writing.

Hedge clauses. A clause that tries to make the client waive rights under the securities laws, or that limits the adviser's liability in a way that could make the client believe they have given up rights that cannot be waived, is prohibited. Under the USA, any condition that binds a person to waive compliance with the Act is void.

Correspondence, confidentiality and recordkeeping

  • Advisers keep originals of written communications they receive and copies of those they send about recommendations or advice, receiving or disbursing funds or securities, and placing or executing orders. Electronic communications, including email, text messages and chat apps, are included. Using personal devices or unapproved apps ("off-channel communications") for business violates the books-and-records rules.
  • Retention: an IA keeps its books and records for 5 years from the end of the fiscal year of the last entry, with the first 2 years in an appropriate office of the adviser (Advisers Act Rule 204-2; NASAA's rule is similar). Broker-dealer communications are generally kept for 3 years under SEC Rule 17a-4.
  • Confidentiality: revealing a client's identity, affairs or investments to anyone else without the client's consent is unethical, unless the law requires it (for example, a subpoena or a regulator's request).
Exam tip: "Registered" is a fact you may state. "Approved," "endorsed" or "recommended by the Administrator" is always a violation.
keyPoints: Stating the fact of registration is fine; implying that the Administrator or SEC approved the firm, its merits or its strategy is unlawful.
NASAA: advisory contracts must be in writing and disclose services, term, fee and formula, prepaid-fee refund, discretion, and no assignment without consent.
USA contract provisions: no performance fee (except for qualified clients), no assignment without client consent, and a partnership IA must notify clients of membership changes.
A change in a minority of partners requires notice only; a change of control is an assignment and requires client consent.
Hedge clauses that waive or appear to waive clients' rights under securities laws are prohibited and void.
Guaranteeing against loss is prohibited; a security may be called 'guaranteed' only if a third party actually guarantees principal or interest.
NASAA brochure delivery: 48 hours before signing, or at signing with a 5-business-day penalty-free cancellation right.
IA records: 5 years, the first 2 in an appropriate office; electronic and off-channel communications are covered.

topics.title: Advertising, the SEC Marketing Rule & Social Media
topics.reading:
What counts as advertising

For state-registered advisers, NASAA-based rules define an advertisement broadly: any written communication addressed to more than one person, or any notice or announcement in a publication, on radio or television, or online, that offers investment advisory services, analyses or reports. Websites and social media pages are advertising. Every advertisement is subject to the antifraud standard: nothing false or misleading, and no material facts left out.

The state rules traditionally followed the SEC's old advertising rule. They prohibited:

  • testimonials;
  • references to past specific profitable recommendations, unless the ad lists all recommendations for at least the prior year;
  • claims that a chart, graph or formula can, by itself, determine which securities to buy;
  • calling a report or service "free" when it is not free of all conditions.

Some states have since moved toward the SEC approach, so state-registered advisers must follow their own state's rule.

The SEC Marketing Rule (Rule 206(4)-1)

The Marketing Rule took effect in 2021, with a compliance date of November 4, 2022. It replaced the SEC's old advertising and cash-solicitation rules for SEC-registered advisers. An advertisement includes:

  • any communication by the adviser to more than one person (or to even one person if it contains hypothetical performance) that offers the adviser's advisory services to prospects or private fund investors, or offers new services to current clients;
  • any paid testimonial or endorsement.

Three things are excluded: extemporaneous, live, oral communications; one-on-one communications (unless they contain hypothetical performance); and information required by statute or regulation.

Seven general prohibitions. An advertisement may not:

  1. include an untrue statement of material fact, or leave out a material fact needed to keep it from being misleading;
  2. include a material statement of fact that the adviser has no reasonable basis to believe it can substantiate if the SEC asks;
  3. include information that would reasonably be likely to create an untrue or misleading implication;
  4. discuss potential benefits without fair and balanced treatment of the material risks;
  5. refer to specific investment advice in a way that is not fair and balanced;
  6. include or exclude performance results, or present time periods, in a way that is not fair and balanced;
  7. otherwise be materially misleading.

Testimonials, endorsements and ratings

A testimonial is a statement by a current client. An endorsement is a statement by someone who is not a client. The Marketing Rule allows both, but the ad must clearly and prominently disclose:

  • whether the person is a client or not;
  • whether they received cash or non-cash compensation;
  • a brief statement of any material conflicts of interest.

The adviser must also oversee compliance. Paid promoters need a written agreement, except for de minimis compensation ($1,000 or less over 12 months) and affiliated promoters. Certain disqualified ("bad actor") persons cannot be paid promoters. Third-party ratings are allowed if the adviser reasonably believes the survey was not designed to produce a set result, and the ad discloses the date of the rating, the period it covers, who gave it, and whether the adviser paid for it.

Performance advertising

  • Net of fees: gross performance may be shown only if net performance is shown with at least equal prominence, over the same period and using the same method.
  • Time periods: performance of any portfolio (other than a private fund) must include 1-, 5- and 10-year periods, or the portfolio's life if shorter. Each period must end on a date no earlier than the most recent calendar year-end.
  • No cherry-picking: "related performance" must include all portfolios with substantially similar policies, objectives and strategies. Some may be left out only if the advertised results are not materially higher than they would be with all of them included. "Extracted" performance (a subset of one portfolio) must come with the total portfolio's results, or an offer to provide them.
  • Hypothetical performance (model or backtested results) is allowed only if the adviser has policies and procedures reasonably designed to make sure it is relevant to the intended audience's likely financial situation and objectives, and it explains the assumptions and risks. In practice, this keeps it away from mass retail audiences.
  • An ad may never say or imply that the SEC has approved or reviewed the performance results.

Social media and websites

  • Adoption: a firm that explicitly or implicitly endorses third-party content becomes responsible for it as though it were the firm's own. Examples include sharing a post, "liking" it to promote it, commenting approvingly, or showing only favorable reviews.
  • Entanglement: a firm that helps prepare third-party content, for example by drafting, editing or paying for it, is responsible for it.
  • Linking to a third-party site the firm knows, or has reason to know, is false or misleading counts as adoption.
  • A client review on an independent site that the firm leaves alone is not the firm's advertisement.
  • FINRA (broker-dealers): static content, such as profiles and banner ads, is a retail communication and needs principal pre-approval. Interactive real-time posts are treated like correspondence: they are supervised and retained but not pre-approved.
  • FINRA categories: correspondence goes to 25 or fewer retail investors within 30 days; a retail communication goes to more than 25. Business communications on social media must be retained.
Trap: "Testimonials are always illegal" is the old rule. Under the SEC Marketing Rule they are allowed with disclosures. Read carefully whether a question is about an SEC-registered adviser or a state rule.
keyPoints: An advertisement is a communication to more than one person offering advisory services; websites and social media count.
SEC Marketing Rule: testimonials (clients) and endorsements (non-clients) are allowed with clear and prominent disclosure of client status, compensation and conflicts.
Gross performance must be accompanied by net performance with at least equal prominence, over the same period and using the same method.
Required periods: 1, 5 and 10 years (or the portfolio's life if shorter), ending no earlier than the most recent calendar year-end.
Cherry-picking is prohibited: related performance must include all substantially similar portfolios unless the exclusion does not materially raise results.
Hypothetical performance requires policies ensuring it is relevant to the intended audience, plus disclosure of assumptions and risks.
Third-party content becomes the firm's through adoption (endorsing or sharing) or entanglement (helping prepare it).
FINRA: static social content needs principal pre-approval; interactive content is supervised like correspondence.

topics.title: Compensation: Fees, Performance Fees, Soft Dollars & Principal Trades
topics.reading:
Advisory fees

Advisers may charge a percentage of assets under management (AUM), an hourly fee, a flat or fixed fee, a retainer, or commissions if the IAR is also registered as an agent. Whatever the structure, the fee must be disclosed in Form ADV Part 2A and in the contract, and it must be reasonable. NASAA lists charging an unreasonable advisory fee as an unethical practice. If a client ends the contract early, unearned prepaid fees must be refunded.

Wrap fees combine advisory, execution and custody costs into a single fee, usually a percentage of assets. Sponsors deliver a special wrap-fee brochure. A wrap account can be unsuitable for a buy-and-hold client who rarely trades, because that client would pay less with commissions plus an advisory fee. Putting such a client into a wrap account is sometimes called "reverse churning."

12b-1 fees and revenue sharing create conflicts. The SEC has sanctioned many advisers for putting clients in mutual fund share classes that pay 12b-1 fees to the adviser or its affiliate when a cheaper share class of the same fund was available, without disclosing the conflict. Doing so breaches the fiduciary duties of loyalty and care.

Performance-based fees

Advisers Act Section 205, and the USA, generally prohibit compensation based on a share of capital gains or capital appreciation. Rule 205-3 makes an exception for qualified clients. A qualified client has either:

  • at least $1.4 million under management with the adviser immediately after signing the contract; or
  • a net worth of more than $2.7 million (alone or jointly with a spouse), excluding the value of the primary residence, when the contract is signed.

Qualified purchasers and certain knowledgeable employees of the adviser also qualify. The SEC adjusts these dollar thresholds for inflation about every five years. The figures above took effect June 29, 2026, replacing the 2021 figures of $1.1 million and $2.2 million; contracts signed before that date are grandfathered, and exam items may still use the older numbers. The exam cares about the concept: performance fees are for wealthier, qualified clients only.

Worked example: Maria has $1.2 million with the adviser. Her net worth is $3.1 million, including $500,000 of equity in her home. Her net worth excluding the home is $3.1 million − $0.5 million = $2.6 million, which does not exceed $2.7 million. Her AUM of $1.2 million is below $1.4 million. She is not a qualified client, so she cannot be charged a performance fee.

Exam tip: A fee based on the average asset value over a period, such as 1% of average quarterly AUM, is not a performance fee, even though it rises when the account grows. A performance fee shares in gains, for example "20% of the account's appreciation."

Soft dollars and Section 28(e)

"Soft dollars" are brokerage and research services an adviser receives from a broker-dealer in return for directing client trades to that broker. Section 28(e) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 creates a safe harbor. An adviser does not breach its fiduciary duty by paying more than the lowest available commission if it decides in good faith that the commission is reasonable relative to the value of the brokerage and research services it receives.

Eligible (helps investment decisions)Not eligible (overhead)
Research reports on companies, industries or the economyOffice rent, utilities, furniture
Analytical and portfolio-modeling softwareTravel, lodging and meals to attend seminars
Financial newsletters, market data and databasesSalaries, marketing and general office computers
Seminar or conference fees for research contentMembership dues, accounting and legal fees

Mixed-use items, such as a data terminal used partly for research and partly for administration, must be allocated: only the research share may be paid with soft dollars. Research does not have to benefit the specific account whose commissions paid for it, but it must benefit clients. Soft-dollar arrangements must be disclosed in Form ADV Part 2A. If a client directs brokerage to a particular broker, the adviser must disclose that the client may not get best execution.

Principal and agency cross transactions

A principal transaction is one where the adviser, acting for its own account, knowingly buys a security from or sells a security to an advisory client. Under Advisers Act Section 206(3) and NASAA, the adviser must disclose in writing the capacity in which it is acting and get the client's consent before the transaction is completed, for each transaction. Blanket advance consent is not enough, and disclosing on the confirmation after the trade is too late.

An agency cross transaction is one where the adviser, or an affiliated broker-dealer, acts as broker for both the advisory client and the party on the other side. It is permitted when:

  • the client gives prospective (blanket) written consent after full disclosure;
  • each trade confirmation discloses the adviser's capacity and pay;
  • the client receives an annual summary of these transactions and the commissions;
  • every disclosure reminds the client that consent can be revoked at any time.

The adviser may not use an agency cross when it recommended the trade to both sides.

Trap: Principal trade = consent for each trade, obtained before completion. Agency cross = blanket written consent allowed, revocable at any time.
keyPoints: Fees must be disclosed and reasonable; charging an unreasonable fee is an unethical practice, and unearned prepaid fees must be refunded.
Wrap fees bundle advisory and execution costs and can be unsuitable for low-trading, buy-and-hold clients.

Performance fees are allowed only for qualified clients: at least $1.4M AUM with the adviser, or net worth over $2.7M excluding the primary residence (SEC thresholds effective June 29, 2026; previously $1.1M/$2.2M; inflation-adjusted about every 5 years).
A fee based on average AUM over a period is not a performance fee.
Section 28(e) safe harbor: research and brokerage that aid investment decisions qualify; rent, furniture, travel and salaries do not; soft dollars must be disclosed.
Principal trades: written disclosure of capacity and client consent before completion of each trade.
Agency cross trades: blanket written consent, per-trade confirmations, annual summary, revocable at any time; not allowed if the adviser recommended both sides.
Choosing a higher-cost 12b-1 share class without disclosure when a cheaper class was available breaches fiduciary duty.

topics.title: Custody of Client Funds & Securities
topics.reading:
What custody means

An adviser has custody when it holds client funds or securities, directly or indirectly, or has any authority to get possession of them. Under the NASAA model custody rule, which is modeled on SEC Rule 206(4)-2, custody arises from three sources:

  • Possession: holding client cash or securities, or holding client checks made payable to the adviser.
  • An arrangement giving authority to withdraw: a general power of attorney; check-writing or signing authority over a client account; automatic deduction of advisory fees from client accounts; a standing letter of authorization (SLOA) that lets the adviser send client money to third parties; or holding a client's username and password when that access allows withdrawals.
  • A legal capacity: acting as general partner of a limited partnership, managing member of an LLC, or trustee of a client's trust.

Inadvertent receipt is not custody if the adviser returns the funds or securities to the sender promptly, and in any case within 3 business days. A limited trading authorization (discretion to buy and sell) is not custody, because it does not let the adviser take money out.

Requirements when an adviser has custody (NASAA model rule)

  1. Notify the Administrator promptly, on Form ADV, that it has or may have custody. No prior approval is required.
  2. Use a qualified custodian, such as a bank, a registered broker-dealer or a futures commission merchant. Assets are held in a separate account for each client under the client's name, or in accounts under the adviser's name as agent or trustee for its clients.
  3. Tell the client in writing the custodian's name, address and how the assets are held, both when the account is opened and whenever this changes.
  4. Account statements at least quarterly. The adviser must have a reasonable basis, after due inquiry, for believing the qualified custodian sends each client a statement at least quarterly. The statement shows the funds and each security held at the end of the period and all transactions during it. If the adviser also sends its own statements, they must urge clients to compare them with the custodian's.
  5. Surprise examination. An independent certified public accountant verifies the client funds and securities through an actual examination, at least once each calendar year, at a time chosen by the accountant without prior notice to the adviser. The accountant files the required report with the Administrator.

Custody only because fees are deducted

Most advisers have custody only because fees come straight out of client accounts. Under the NASAA model rule, those advisers must meet three safeguards:

  • have the client's written authorization to deduct fees;
  • send the qualified custodian written notice of the fee amount each time;
  • at the same time, send the client an itemized invoice showing the fee, the formula, the period covered, and the asset value it was based on.

Advisers whose only custody comes from fee deduction are generally excused from the surprise examination.

Pooled investment vehicles

When the adviser is the general partner of a limited partnership (or similar pooled vehicle), sending quarterly statements to investors can be replaced by sending audited financial statements, prepared under GAAP, to all investors within 120 days after the fiscal year-end.

Financial requirements (NASAA)

State-registered adviser that…Minimum net worth
has custody$35,000
has discretion but not custody$10,000
accepts prepayment of more than $500 per client, 6 or more months in advance (no custody or discretion)Positive net worth

Custody may also trigger bonding requirements under state rules.

Trap: Discretion lets you trade an account. Custody means you can withdraw from it. A limited trading authorization is not custody, but fee deduction, a general power of attorney, check-writing authority and serving as trustee are.
Exam tip: Memorize the custody numbers: 3 business days to return property received by mistake, quarterly custodian statements, a surprise exam once a calendar year, and 120 days for pooled-fund audited financials.
keyPoints: Custody means holding client assets or having authority to obtain them: fee deduction, general POA, check-writing, SLOA, withdrawal-capable passwords, trustee or GP roles.
Inadvertent receipt is not custody if the property is returned to the sender within 3 business days.
With custody: notify the Administrator on Form ADV, use a qualified custodian, and tell clients in writing where the assets are held.
Qualified custodian statements go to clients at least quarterly; the adviser needs a reasonable basis to believe they are sent.
An independent CPA conducts a surprise examination at least once each calendar year; fee-deduction-only advisers are generally exempt.
Fee deduction safeguards: written client authorization, fee notice to the custodian, and an itemized invoice to the client.
Pooled vehicles can instead deliver audited financial statements within 120 days of fiscal year-end.
NASAA minimum net worth: $35,000 with custody; $10,000 with discretion only.

topics.title: Discretionary Authority & Trading Authorization
topics.reading:
What discretion is

A person exercises discretion when they decide, without asking the client first, any of the "three A's":

  • Asset: which security to buy or sell;
  • Action: whether to buy or sell;
  • Amount: how many shares or bonds.

Deciding only the time or price of an order is not discretion. If a client says "buy 1,000 shares of ABC today, use your judgment on timing and price," the client has chosen the asset, the action and the amount. The representative only has time-and-price discretion.

Written authorization: IAs versus broker-dealer agents

PersonWhen written discretionary authority is required
Investment adviser or IAR (NASAA IA statement of policy)May act on oral authority at first, but must get written authority within 10 business days after the first discretionary transaction
Broker-dealer or agent (NASAA BD statement of policy)Must get written authority before the first discretionary trade

Time-and-price discretion does not need written authorization. Under FINRA Rule 3260, it is limited to the business day it is granted. An unfilled order expires at the end of that day unless the client gives written authorization saying otherwise.

Duties that continue after discretion is granted

  • Suitability and objectives still apply. Discretion does not let the adviser ignore the client's stated objectives, risk tolerance or restrictions.
  • No excessive trading. NASAA lists as unethical any transactions that are excessive in size or frequency given the client's financial resources, objectives and the character of the account. In a discretionary account, excessive trading for commissions is churning.
  • Supervision. Broker-dealers must have a principal promptly approve discretionary orders in writing and review discretionary accounts frequently.
  • Third-party instructions. Accepting orders from anyone other than the client, such as a spouse or adult child, without the client's written third-party trading authorization is unethical. Oral permission is not enough.

Unauthorized trading

In a non-discretionary account, every trade needs the client's approval before it is placed. Placing a trade without that approval is unauthorized trading and is unethical even if the trade makes money. The client cannot "consent" by approving after the fact. A representative who acts first and asks later has already violated the rules.

Discretion is not custody

A limited (trading) power of attorney allows buying and selling in the account. It does not allow withdrawing money, so it gives discretion without custody. A full or general power of attorney that allows withdrawals creates custody. Under the NASAA net capital and net worth rules, an adviser with discretion (but no custody) must keep a minimum net worth of $10,000, compared with $35,000 for custody.

Other points

  • The Form ADV brochure must say whether the adviser has discretionary authority, and the written contract must state whether it grants discretionary power.
  • A client may put limits on discretion, for example no tobacco stocks or no options. The adviser must follow them.
  • Discretionary authority ends when the client revokes it, and it generally ends when the client dies. A power of attorney ends at death; the executor then acts for the estate.
Trap: The 10-business-day grace period is for investment advisers. An agent of a broker-dealer who trades on oral discretion before getting written authority has committed an unethical practice, even if the paperwork arrives the next day.
Exam tip: If the client named the security, the direction and the quantity, anything left over (time or price) is not discretion.
keyPoints: Discretion covers asset, action or amount; time and price alone are not discretion.
IAs and IARs: written discretionary authority is due within 10 business days after the first discretionary trade (NASAA).
Broker-dealer agents: written discretionary authority must be obtained before the first discretionary trade.
Time-and-price discretion expires at the end of the business day it is granted, unless written authorization says otherwise (FINRA 3260).
Unauthorized trading in a non-discretionary account is unethical even if the trade is profitable.
Excessive trading in a discretionary account (churning) is unethical; discretion never overrides the client's objectives.
Taking orders from a third party requires the client's written third-party trading authorization.
A limited trading authorization is discretion without custody; a general POA that allows withdrawals creates custody.
